body:
The 0.3.3 release rehearsal (run 39231145358 at 534e7d6) passes only on Linux x86_64. Windows x86_64 MSVC, macOS x86_64 and macOS arm64 each fail 132 to 151 tests in the expression semantics corpus, the planar numeric replay, the construction corpus and related families.

Each failure traces to a last-bit difference in a transcendental function. For example, `acos(0.3301...)` ends in `...711` on Linux and `...710` on the other platforms. The crates call each platform's C math library, either through `martensite-cmath` or through `f64` methods such as `sin`, `acos`, `exp` and `powf` that lower to it. The expected values were recorded on Linux with glibc, which is not correctly rounded for every function. Constant arguments are also folded at compile time with the build host's math library.

Decision (2026-10-19): every transcendental function in every crate goes through one portable, correctly rounded binary64 library behind `martensite-cmath`. Results then match bit for bit on Linux x86_64, Windows x86_64 MSVC, macOS x86_64 and macOS arm64. This replaces the platform-native profile considered in #198.

Acceptance:

- `martensite-cmath` owns every transcendental function the crates use. The functions are correctly rounded, have spot tests against high-precision references and are pinned to an exact dependency version.
- No crate calls the standard `f64`/`f32` transcendental methods directly. Clippy `disallowed-methods` in `clippy.toml` enforces this in `cargo xtask pr`.
- Expected values change only where glibc was not correctly rounded. Each changed value is shown to equal the correctly rounded result (computed with high-precision arithmetic) and is listed in a reviewed baseline record with a new behavior version. Every request, assertion and tolerance stays.
- The release rehearsal passes on all four release targets.
title: Make transcendental results identical on every release platform
